questions.heading: A Table Over Budget Amounts Finds the Best Plan
questions.stem: A planner has 200 candidate projects and one budget of $50,000,000, every cost in whole dollars, and runs the best-value table with $1 steps. Roughly how much work does the table take?

options.text: About 2^200, since the table lists every plan of the projects
options.says: The table never lists plans; it keeps one best value per budget amount.

options.text: About 200 × 50,000,000, since the work grows with the budget's size
options.says: Right: one step per item per budget step, so the work grows with the budget as a number (pseudo-polynomial).

options.text: About 200 × 8, since the work grows with the budget's digits
options.says: The work grows with the budget's size, not its digits: writing GridCap in dollars instead of $10k makes the table ten thousand times longer.

options.text: About 200, since each project is handled in a single step
options.says: Each project updates every budget column, 3,077 of them on GridCap small, not one entry.

questions.heading: With Several Rows, No Single Ratio Ranks the Items
questions.stem: A model has three capacity rows: money, crew-hours and outage days. A colleague sorts the items by value divided by the sum of each item's shares of the three capacities, then takes each item in that order if it still fits all three rows. What does that procedure give?

options.text: The best plan, since the score weighs every row at once
options.says: The scaled-use rule on GridCap small ended $328k below the optimum; no single score knows in advance which rows will be tight.

options.text: A plan that may break a row, since the score mixes the rows
options.says: An item is taken only if it still fits every row, so the plan always keeps all three.

options.text: A plan that keeps each row, though it may not be the best
options.says: Right: a greedy fill keeps every row but, with several rows, can miss the optimum, as all three rules did on GridCap small.

options.text: The LP relaxation's value, since a ratio fill solves the LP
options.says: A ratio fill solves the LP of a one-row knapsack only; with several rows the LP needs a solver and has up to one fraction per row.

questions.heading: With Several Rows, No Single Ratio Ranks the Items
questions.stem: The LP relaxation of a knapsack with 50 items and 4 capacity rows is solved, and the solver returns a vertex. At most how many items can that solution leave strictly between 0 and 1?

options.text: 1, the split item, whatever the number of rows
options.says: One split item is the one-row case; GridCap small's six-row LP had four fractional projects.

options.text: 46, the items left over once the 4 rows are tight
options.says: It is the other way round: at least 50 - 4 of the tight constraints at a vertex are bounds, so at least 46 items sit at 0 or 1.

options.text: 50, since any item may take a fractional value
options.says: At a vertex, 50 constraints are tight and only 4 of them can be rows; the other items sit at a bound.

options.text: 4, since at most one per row can be fractional
options.says: Right: at most m variables, one per row, are fractional at a vertex of an m-row knapsack.
